title: Agentic Evaluations and Long Horizon Tasks
summary: Classic chatbot/QA/single-shot benchmarks saturate and cannot track agentic progress, so this lecture builds a framework for evaluating long-horizon autonomy along three axes: task duration, real-world economic value, and research-synthesis quality. It walks METR's human-calibrated time horizon (SWAA/EdgeCast/RE-Bench, ~170 tasks from 1s to 8h, doubling every ~7 months at 50% success, far shorter at 80%), OpenAI's GDPval (pairwise win rate vs decade-experienced professionals on top-5%-of-GDP tasks, rising roughly linearly to ~48%), and Stanford's DeepScholarBench (live, contamination-resistant related-work synthesis where no system exceeds 19%). Recurring gaps are reliability, context/reference-data grounding, error recovery, and faithful instruction following rather than raw task length.

sections.title: Framing: What Counts as an Agentic Evaluation
sections.problem: Most practitioners run no formal evaluation, and the ones who do reach for short, single-purpose tasks that say little about long-horizon autonomy.
sections.why: The field lacks a shared definition of an agentic eval; ad-hoc task choices vary wildly in horizon, tool use, and grounding, so they cannot track progress.
sections.how: The instructor polls the room, collects concrete eval examples, then lays out the lecture's three anchor papers: METR, GDPval, and DeepScholarBench.
sections.detail:
The instructor opens by polling who has run an evaluation and what tasks they used. Answers cluster around multihop QA (HotpotQA-style), SweBench, and an agent that distills a private wiki into notes before feeding a coding agent.

  • The framing question is what makes agentic evaluations hard relative to prior evaluation regimes.
  • Three anchor papers structure the lecture: METR (time horizon of completable tasks), GDPval (real-world economically valuable tasks, OpenAI), and DeepScholarBench (live generative research synthesis, Stanford).
  • These evals differ along task duration, economic value, and grounding in reference data; each is a distinct measurement axis.
  • They are also more expensive and higher-variance than chat/QA suites because they require tool loops and human grading.
  • The instructor warns that any benchmark is a representation of what we believe is measurable, not ground truth.

sections.title: Why Measure: Saturation, Capability, and Economic Value
sections.problem: Traditional chatbot, question-answering, and single-shot benchmarks whose answer is already in context are saturating quickly.
sections.why: We must forecast capability and economic/safety impact, and shallow in-context recall scores no longer discriminate frontier agents.
sections.how: Track two complementary metrics -- METR's human-calibrated time horizon (capability) and GDPval's win rate vs experts (economic value) -- then add a third for research synthesis.
sections.detail:
The instructor frames the core challenge: to assess AI progress we must measure what matters, and what matters now spans both capability and economic/safety impact.

  • Four to five years ago, merely generating a fluent explanation was a milestone; today we ask whether models affect economics or safety.
  • Traditional benchmarks -- chatbots, question answering, and single-shot tasks whose answer is already in context -- are saturating quickly.
  • Two complementary metrics are introduced: METR measures the time horizon of tasks (how long or complex a task a model can finish), calibrated by human professionals; GDPval measures the model's win rate versus experts on real work.
  • Both are equally valid and yield similar qualitative insights, but the trends they measure differ -- exponential versus roughly linear.
  • A third metric, research-synthesis quality, is added via DeepScholarBench.

sections.title: The Time Horizon: Duration plus Reliability
sections.problem: A raw can-the-model-do-this question is too coarse; there is no unit of how long a model can keep working or how often it succeeds.
sections.why: Chatbots lost context after a few turns, so sustained multi-turn work is itself new; and duration without reliability is meaningless for deployment.
sections.how: METR measures task duration and associates a reliability level (e.g. 50% or 80% success) with it, anchored to how long human professionals need.
sections.detail:
The horizon framing starts from a concrete observation: three to five years ago a chatbot would lose the thread after a couple of turns, whereas today conversations stay coherent over long multi-turn exchanges. That contextual endurance is the raw substrate for long-horizon work.

  • METR therefore measures two things: the duration of the task the model can complete and the reliability with which it does so.
  • Reliability is reported as a success threshold -- e.g. completion with 50% success versus 80% success.
  • The universal anchor for difficulty is how long a human professional takes on the same task, making durations comparable across domains.
  • Horizon is not a single number: the 50%-reliability and 80%-reliability horizons can differ by an order of magnitude.

sections.title: METR's Three Suites, from Seconds to Eight Hours
sections.problem: No single task set spans the full range from atomic software actions to multi-hour ML research.
sections.why: To fit a horizon curve you need tasks whose human completion times cover several orders of magnitude.
sections.how: METR combines three suites -- SWAA (1-30s atomic), EdgeCast (1 min-30h diverse SWE/research), RE-Bench (up to 8h ML research) -- about 170 tasks total.
sections.detail:
METR assembles three suites to span the duration range:

  • SWAA-style small suite: 1-30 seconds, purely atomic software actions (e.g. open a file) -- about 66 tasks.
  • EdgeCast: 1 minute to ~30 hours of diverse software and research engineering tasks -- about 97 tasks.
  • RE-Bench: full ML research tasks up to about 8 hours (AI-scientist style) -- only about 7 tasks.
  • In total roughly 170 tasks from one second to eight hours, mapped onto a single duration axis.
  • Example tasks span finding a shell script (~3 s) through detecting and fixing a bug in a simulation's input files (~10 min) to implementing custom CUDA kernels to a performance target (tens of hours, capped near 8 h).
  • The spread lets success rate be plotted smoothly against human time.

sections.title: Constructing the Curve from Human Completion Times
sections.problem: Turning raw task outcomes into a single horizon number requires a principled aggregation pipeline.
sections.why: A model may pass some tasks and fail others in the same human-time bucket, so per-task results must be summarized into a curve.
sections.how: Collect and vet tasks, record human and agent time estimates, then fit success rate against human time and read off the horizon at a chosen reliability.
sections.detail:
The horizon number is produced by a pipeline, not a single score:

  • Tasks are collected and vetted for each suite so the suite is representative.
  • For each task, human runs estimate completion time and difficulty; agent runs measure whether the task is completed reliably.
  • Given enough data points, METR fits a curve of success rate versus human time estimate and reads off the horizon at a chosen reliability.
  • Horizons are then plotted against model release dates, yielding the trend the lecture examines next.
  • This design makes a single time-horizon number meaningful, but the number also inherits every bias in the human estimates and in the fit.

sections.title: Class Calibration: What Takes Minutes vs Hours
sections.problem: Students must calibrate which duration bucket a realistic task actually falls into.
sections.why: Suite assignment depends on human completion time, and students systematically underestimate how long real tasks take.
sections.how: The instructor solicits minute-scale and hour-scale tasks students would delegate, then maps each to SWAA, EdgeCast, or RE-Bench.
sections.detail:
To build intuition, the instructor asks students for a task taking a couple of minutes and one taking a couple of hours that they would delegate.

  • A several-hour task lands in EdgeCast or RE-Bench territory.
  • Double-checking a bibliography entry by querying the right websites maps to the EdgeCast-style diverse-task bucket.
  • Refactoring code can be small or large: moving code while preserving logic may take a few hours to a couple of days, and someone must verify correctness -- pushing it toward RE-Bench.
  • The exercise shows that suite assignment depends on human completion time, not on how a task "feels."
  • It also surfaces a recurring theme: verification cost is often the hidden part of a task's true duration.

sections.title: Human Baselines: Experts, Agreement, Cost, and Bias
sections.problem: Human completion time is the universal anchor, but it varies across people and is expensive to collect at scale.
sections.why: Many experts per task is costly, the estimate is a distribution rather than a point, and expert self-assessment is systematically biased.
sections.how: Use a few skilled professionals (~5 years experience), record successful-attempt times, take a geometric mean for difficulty, check inter-human agreement, and gather more points only when estimates diverge.
sections.detail:
Human completion time is the anchor, but it is a distribution and expensive to collect.

  • Rather than many experts, METR typically has a few skilled professionals (~5 years experience) solve each task, records times on successful attempts, and takes a geometric mean as the difficulty rating.
  • Inter-human agreement is checked; more data points are gathered only when estimates diverge. Many experts would give a better distribution but cost far more.
  • Example ladder: find a shell script (~3 s); Wikipedia research; detect/fix a bug in simulation input files (~10 min); munging JSON between formats; implement custom CUDA kernels to a target (up to ~8 h).
  • Expert bias: experienced annotators are conditioned to know what "success" means and often underestimate difficulty, which may not match how a model perceives the task.

sections.title: The Horizon Plot and the Seven-Month Doubling
sections.problem: It is unclear whether models really complete ever-longer tasks or whether reported gains are artifacts of easy tasks.
sections.why: A success-rate-versus-duration curve across suites and release dates is needed to see a trend and explain which capabilities move it.
sections.how: Plot success against human time, read the horizon at 50% success, compare release dates, and attribute gains to reasoning, code, tools, reliability, error recovery, and context engineering.
sections.detail:
On the horizon plot, the x-axis is human completion time and the y-axis is model success rate.

  • SWAA (small) tasks generally sit high; EdgeCast tasks scatter from about 0.8 down to 0; RE-Bench tasks sit low -- longer tasks are harder to stay on track with.
  • Reading the horizon at 50% success by release date: GPT-2 (2019) ~2 seconds; GPT-4 (2023) ~8 minutes; Claude 3.7 Sonnet (2025) up to 59 minutes -- an apparent doubling roughly every 7 months.
  • The caveat: 50% success means the model fails half the time -- like an intern who only sometimes returns an answer, so uncertainty always remains.
  • Drivers include better logical reasoning, code generation, tool use (ReAct), non-repetitive reliability, error recovery, goal awareness/memory of progress, and context engineering.

sections.title: What Drives Progress: Reasoning, Code, Tools, Recovery
sections.problem: The horizon trend needs a mechanism; it is not obvious which capabilities produce longer autonomous runs.
sections.why: Longer tasks compound errors, so progress requires more than better next-token quality.
sections.how: Attribute gains to improved logical reasoning, code generation, tool use (ReAct), non-repetitive reliability, error recovery, goal/state awareness, and context management.
sections.detail:
Why do horizons keep growing? The instructor attributes the improvement to several concrete capabilities rather than scale alone.

  • Logical reasoning: models learned to reason in ways covered by earlier lectures, which helps decompose and execute multi-step tasks.
  • Code generation: stronger coding drives gains on SWE and ML-research suites.
  • Tool use: ReAct-style tool selection and invocation is now more reliable.
  • Reliability: models repeat behavior less often and avoid getting stuck.
  • Error recovery: an 8-hour task will contain wrong steps, so the model must detect and recover from them.
  • Goal awareness and memory: the model must track the final goal and how far it has progressed.
  • Context engineering: managing context across many steps (compaction, planning, replanning) is itself a major driver.

sections.title: Class Discussion: Context Engineering, Compaction, Replanning
sections.problem: Why do coding agents such as Claude Code improve year over year?
sections.why: Mechanisms inside the agent loop, not just the base model, determine long-horizon success.
sections.how: Collect student explanations: context engineering, compaction, planning/replanning, user-feedback loops, online RL from logs, and memory of the environment.
sections.detail:
The instructor asks why Claude Code and similar coding agents are better today than a year ago, and collects several mechanisms.

  • Context engineering: structuring context better across many steps is a new discipline that improves the tooling.
  • Compaction: when the context window fills, the agent summarizes and compresses history and continues.
  • Planning and replanning: on complex problems the agent first breaks the task into steps, and when execution reveals new data it may generate a new set of steps.
  • User feedback: when the user says the output is wrong, the agent redoes the work -- like an assignment sent back.
  • Online RL from user logs: students speculate products such as Cursor learn from real usage logs.
  • Memory of the environment: understanding the codebase helps the agent once it has operated there before.

sections.title: The Reliability Axis: The 50% vs 80% Horizon Gap
sections.problem: A 59-minute horizon sounds deployable until you demand confidence: at 80% success the same model sustains far less.
sections.why: Capability and reliability are separate axes; a 50% success rate is unacceptable when a failed run has real cost.
sections.how: Report multiple reliability curves (gray = 50%, blue = 80%) and compare horizons at each; the gap quantifies headroom for systems built on top of the model.
sections.detail:
The reliability view re-plots the same horizon data with a higher bar.

  • The gray line is 50% reliability; the blue line is 80% success rate. x-axis is release date, y-axis is model time-to-complete.
  • For Claude 3.7 Sonnet, the 50% horizon is 59 minutes, but the 80% horizon is roughly 15 minutes (one plot suggests 8-10 minutes) -- a large delta.
  • The doubling time (~7 months) is similar on both curves, but the absolute deployable duration is far lower at 80%.
  • Implication: deploying models on real tasks hits reliability challenges even for moderately complex tasks, leaving headroom for systems built on top (verification, retries, tools).
  • This is also a cost/variance problem: failed attempts consume tokens and wall-clock time, and low success rates multiply them.

sections.title: Failure Modes of Long-Horizon Agents
sections.problem: Long tasks compound errors, but it is unclear which failure categories dominate and whether reasoning models fix them.
sections.why: Reaching a goal over many steps requires correct decomposition, tool choice, and global state awareness.
sections.how: METR classified failures on a non-reasoning model (GPT-4o) versus a reasoning model (o1): poor planning, poor tool choice, incorrect reasoning, premature abandonment, and repetitive loops.
sections.detail:
METR's failure analysis compares a non-reasoning model (GPT-4o) with a reasoning model (o1); the categories are the learning signal.

  • Poor planning: the model fails to break the given task into steps.
  • Poor tool choice: it selects an inappropriate tool or malformed call.
  • Incorrect mental math / reasoning: it attempts reasoning but gets it wrong.
  • Premature abandonment: it loops on repetitive behavior and cannot determine what success means.
  • Repetitive loops: after an action fails it remains the highest-probability action, so the model repeats it; this was high for GPT-4o and lower for o1.
  • Failure-mode analysis is standard on hard benchmarks and is exactly the self-refinement homework task: find where the agent's loop broke down.
  • These modes (planning, tool choice, goal detection, loops) map directly onto the capabilities needed for longer horizons.

sections.title: METR's Limitations: Messiness, Contamination, Contractors
sections.problem: Horizon scores are optimistic proxies, distorted by distribution mismatch and training-data contamination.
sections.why: Suites reward clean, verifiable outcomes; models have seen public repos; annotators underestimate durations; and models lack an expert's accumulated context.
sections.how: Treat the numbers as bounded: expect lower messy-task performance, discount contamination-prone suites, and compare model behavior against low-context humans (contractors).
sections.detail:
The instructor stresses that no benchmark is perfect; METR is a first attempt at measuring time horizon and has three concrete limitations.

  • Messiness: performance is lower on tasks with no single correct answer or extra complexity, though similar trend shapes recur across categories.
  • Contamination: on SWE-bench the models have seen most public GitHub repositories and annotators underestimate durations, so estimates are shorter than they would be on unseen repos.
  • Context gap: for internal pull requests, contractors (no codebase context) are 5-18x slower than maintainers, and model performance tracks closer to contractor times.
  • Implication: the model operates as a low-context worker, valuable but not an area expert; when accumulated context matters, the model is at a disadvantage.

sections.title: GDPval: Scoring Real Work Against Experts
sections.problem: Horizon metrics say nothing about economic usefulness, and there was no quantitative way to measure which professional tasks models can do.
sections.why: Real work is subjective, multimodal, and context-heavy, so it cannot be reduced to pass/fail unit tests.
sections.how: GDPval sources real deliverables from professionals with 10+ years experience and scores models by pairwise win rate against those experts.
sections.detail:
GDPval (OpenAI) flips the question: if a task were handed to the model instead of a professional, is the output good enough?

  • Tasks are real deliverables sourced from professionals with 10+ years of experience across a broad set of industries.
  • Scoring is a pairwise win rate against those experts, reported as wins+ties and wins-only preferences.
  • Because the models are multimodal, the suite includes video, CAD, audio, spreadsheets, and presentations, not just text.
  • The design deliberately accepts subjectivity: real work is evaluated relative to a human expert rather than a single ground-truth answer, capturing whether output is useful rather than exactly right.

sections.title: GDPval Example Tasks Across Professions
sections.problem: Concrete examples are needed to judge which real deliverables are tractable.
sections.why: Task realism and subjectivity determine whether a win rate is meaningful.
sections.how: Walk through the suite: manufacturing, finance, nursing, video editing, customer service, concierge, audit, real estate, and recreation tasks, all sourced from professionals.
sections.detail:
Concrete tasks make the abstraction tangible; all are sourced from professionals in their fields.

  • Manufacturing engineer: design a 3D model of a cable-reel stand for an assembly line.
  • Financial/investment analyst: create the competitive landscape (research heavy).
  • Registered nurse: assess images of an issue and produce a consultation report.
  • Film/video editor: create an intro reel from a script.
  • Customer service: draft an email response to a dissatisfied customer.
  • Concierge: build an itinerary for a family of four.
  • Auditor: find pricing inconsistencies across purchase orders.
  • Real-estate agent: design a sales brochure for a new property.
  • Recreation worker: optimize the layout for a vendor fair.

These range from objective (audit) to subjective (brochure), which motivates the win-rate metric and the later discussion of context.

sections.title: Subjectivity, Win Rate, and Expert Context
sections.problem: Many real tasks are subjective, so no single correct answer exists and a model's chosen style may not hold for all cases.
sections.why: Real work requires both context and subjective judgment; capability and appropriateness are separate questions.
sections.how: Use pairwise preference versus experts; separate can-models-do-it from should-we-deploy-it; prefer deliverables with a fairly clear working/not-working signal.
sections.detail:
Students note that many tasks are subjective -- there may be no single right answer, and a model's chosen style may not hold for all cases. The instructor agrees and separates concerns.

  • Subjectivity is exactly why GDPval uses a win rate rather than pass/fail, and why real work requires both context and subjective judgment.
  • The instructor separates whether models are good at a task from whether we want to use them for ethics/compliance -- e.g. legal tasks may be capable but not appropriate to delegate.
  • Healthcare examples skew to registered nurses/nurse practitioners rather than doctors; music composition may appear later but is not in the benchmark yet because verification is hard.
  • The discussion favors deliverables with a fairly clear working/not-working signal, which makes grading tractable.

sections.title: GDPval Dataset Anatomy: Top 5% of GDP, 220 Tasks
sections.problem: The suite must represent economically valuable work and be well specified, or win rates reflect prompt artifacts.
sections.why: Coverage and specification determine whether results generalize to the professions the benchmark claims to measure.
sections.how: Build top-down across 9 sectors targeting the top 5% of GDP, 44 occupations and ~220 gold tasks, with multimodal artifacts and expert vetting.
sections.detail:
The suite is built top-down to be economically representative:

  • 9 sectors chosen to target the top 5% of GDP -- the most economically valuable tasks.
  • 44 occupations and roughly 220 tasks in the open gold set, with about 60% of computer-based O*NET tasks included.
  • Task characteristics: average completion up to ~7 hours, some spanning weeks; text plus multimodal artifacts (CAD, video, audio, spreadsheets, presentations); average task value around $400.
  • About 70% of tasks require interacting with reference files to reach the final output.
  • About 89% of tasks were vetted by experts as well specified -- not ill-specified traps that would fail models for the wrong reason.

sections.title: GDPval Trend: Linear Win-Rate Growth
sections.problem: Economic win rate improves far more slowly than METR's exponential horizon story suggests.
sections.why: Real work requires tacit knowledge and faithful reference-data use, so models cannot substitute fluent generation for grounding.
sections.how: Plot win rate against model generation, report wins+ties vs wins-only, compare to METR in Q&A, and break results down by profession.
sections.detail:
Win rate versus model generation tells a different story than METR.

  • x-axis: models from GPT-4o through GPT-5-high to Claude Opus 4.1; y-axis: win rate versus an industry professional. Light blue is wins+ties; dark blue is wins only.
  • GPT-4o (2024) averages about 12.4%; by 2025 models reach the 20s-30s; Claude Opus 4.1 reaches about 47.6%.
  • This is a roughly linear trend, not the ~7-month exponential doubling of METR.
  • In Q&A the instructor says the two are not directly comparable -- different metrics -- but GDPval shows that on multi-hour to multi-week, profession-specific real work models are only so reliable.
  • Breaking performance down by profession makes the assessment more realistic than a single hours-based number.

sections.title: Model Strengths, Instruction-Following Failures, Output Quality
sections.problem: The dominant failures are instruction following and grounding, not raw reasoning, and usefulness is capped by context the model lacks.
sections.why: Real tasks are well specified but require tacit knowledge and faithful use of provided reference data.
sections.how: Decompose failures by type and sector, grade output quality, and compare model profiles on aesthetics, formatting, calculations, and text.
sections.detail:
Two analyses dominate this chunk: which models are strong where, and what actually fails.

  • Strengths: some models win on aesthetics, document formatting, PDFs, spreadsheets, and presentations; GPT-5 tends to win on instruction following, correct calculations, and text tasks.
  • Failure modes are dominated by instruction following: models promise to consult reference data but do not, override it with hallucinated content, and make formatting errors. GPT-5 shows fewer reference-data instruction failures.
  • Usefulness distribution: roughly half of tasks are acceptable but subpar if delegated; about 20% are tasks where the model would genuinely be better; about 29% are bad or catastrophic.
  • There is measurable disagreement between human graders, which adds noise to these numbers.

sections.title: Self-Refinement: n Attempts, 1.6x Cost, 1.4x Speed
sections.problem: One-shot win rates understate what iterative self-correction can add.
sections.why: Parallel and sequential sampling with self-correction can recover quality, directly relevant to a self-improving-agents class.
sections.how: Compare a single trial with n attempts where each iteration improves on the last; measure cost and speed versus an unaided expert and against salary.
sections.detail:
Because the course is about self-improving agents, the instructors test iterative self-correction.

  • Protocol: a naive single trial versus n attempts, where in the sequential case each iteration is asked to improve on the previous one (parallel or sequential sampling).
  • Reported gains for GPT-5: about 1.6x cost improvement and about 1.4x speed improvement relative to an unaided expert.
  • Even when successful, the run still costs less than 10% of a human expert's salary -- so a subset of professions is already strongly served.
  • The caveat is that these gains apply where the model is successful; they do not remove the underlying reliability gap, and repeated attempts multiply evaluation cost.
  • This connects the evaluation to the self-improvement theme: sampling plus self-correction is a first-order knob.

sections.title: Sector Variation and Where Models Reach Parity
sections.problem: Aggregate win rate hides large per-occupation variation.
sections.why: Some task categories suit model strengths (digital, text, research) while others require expertise models lack.
sections.how: Compare per-occupation win rates against the red human-expert line and identify where models reach or exceed parity.
sections.detail:
Aggregate win rate hides large variation, so the lecture drills into occupations (red line = human expert; each color = a model).

  • Approaching or at parity: counter/rental clerks, real-estate brokers, shipping/receiving and inventory clerks, buyers and purchasing agents, computer/IT system managers, and software developers.
  • Doing extremely well: government administrative service managers, compliance officers, medical and health service managers, personal financial advisors, customer service representatives, plus sales, editing, investigative/detective, and news-analyst tasks.
  • Caveat on software: the human baseline may be repository maintainers rather than a full decade of experience; in fields such as industrial/mechanical engineering, decade-long expertise matters more.
  • These plots act as a taxonomy of where models are useful today and a starting point for studying failures.

sections.title: Underspecification and the Context Gap
sections.problem: When prompts are underspecified or require gathered context, models cannot figure out what to work on.
sections.why: Real work is context-heavy; humans hold context in their heads and architect the problem, while models cannot yet acquire it autonomously.
sections.how: Test underspecified prompts, compare contractor vs maintainer, frame near-term value as AI assistance with human oversight, and prioritize task categories over dollar value.
sections.detail:
The last GDPval theme is what models cannot do without help.

  • Underspecification: removing context from prompts lowers win rate only a few points, but the model's output quality degrades more because it cannot figure out what to work on.
  • Context gap: a repository maintainer is far faster than an external contractor; models behave like the low-context contractor and cannot gather that context themselves.
  • Hence in real work humans architect the set of problems and supply context; the model then executes. Near-term, AI assistance is cost-effective when coupled with human oversight, and different models suit different task types.
  • On dollar value: the amount matters less than the category of task (deep research, code generation, synthesizing diverse sources); the benchmark is a quantifiable taxonomy of valuable categories.

sections.title: DeepScholarBench: Live Related-Work Synthesis
sections.problem: Real work also requires grounding in knowledge bases, not just long duration or economic value.
sections.why: Models are frozen at a knowledge cutoff, may miss foundational papers, and coherent writing is not the same as coverage or verifiability.
sections.how: DeepScholarBench (Stanford) generates related-work sections from recent PhD-level papers across 22 domains, rerun monthly and restricted to post-training papers; three human-validated axes.
sections.detail:
DeepScholarBench (Stanford) targets the related-work section of a paper -- a task a classmate asked for and that practitioners constantly need.

  • Live and contamination-resistant: built from recent arXiv papers at PhD-level difficulty across 22 domains, rerun monthly with new papers, and restricted to papers published after a major model's training cutoff.
  • Task: retrieve relevant references, synthesize findings into coherent claims, and support them with verifiable citations.
  • Prior art includes OpenAI Deep Research, Gemini Deep Research, Perplexity, Stanford's STORM, and OpenScholar.
  • Three human-validated axes: knowledge synthesis (coherent, captures key facts), retrieval quality (relevance, citation counts, foundational-paper coverage), and verifiability (do citations actually support the claims).
  • Metrics agree with humans about 70-80% of the time.

sections.title: DeepScholarBench Results: No System Above 19%
sections.problem: Despite industrial deep-research prototypes, quality and verifiability remain far below expert level.
sections.why: Success requires finding comprehensive foundational sources, surfacing key facts, and keeping citations faithful -- capabilities current systems lack.
sections.how: Report per-axis scores and failure modes; probe retrieval and synthesis separately; vary whether perfect sources are supplied to isolate the bottleneck.
sections.detail:
Unlike most benchmarks, this one has enormous headroom: no existing system exceeds 19%.

  • Knowledge synthesis: OpenAI Deep Research writes well but almost all models consistently miss key facts -- coherent English without full coverage.
  • Retrieval quality: overall only okay-ish; all systems struggle to find comprehensive and important sources; document importance is below 12.5%.
  • Verifiability: DeepScholarBench reaches up to about 90% precision, but Open Deep Research has lower verifiability despite fluent prose.
  • Failure modes: not finding foundational papers; poor assessment of document importance; even when given the perfect sources, key-fact coverage is only about 50%.
  • Trade-off: no system excels at both synthesis quality and verifiability -- exactly the precision/recall balance an occupation needs.

sections.title: DeepScholarBench Q&A and Synthesis in Horizon Terms
sections.problem: Why single out this narrow task, and how does it relate to horizon and economics?
sections.why: Real-world tasks need knowledge-base grounding, and related work is a representative, economically valuable research-synthesis task.
sections.how: Q&A clarifies claims/citations coverage, then the instructor places synthesis on the horizon axis and attributes gaps to multi-step reasoning, information gathering, verifiability, and context engineering.
sections.detail:
Q&A clarifies the benchmark, then the instructor places it on the horizon axis.

  • Experts provide a list of foundational papers, but the benchmark also checks whether the written claims are supported and which papers back them -- not just the count retrieved.
  • On the METR duration axis, research-synthesis tasks are estimated at 30 minutes to 8 hours, while current capability sits around 50 minutes, often with only ~50% success.
  • A task can look long-horizon on the plot yet produce low-quality, low-verifiability output -- duration and quality are different axes.
  • Gaps come from multi-step reasoning, comprehensive information gathering, and maintaining verifiability while synthesizing.
  • This mirrors homework 3: combining multiple agent calls requires context engineering across distributed sources and repeated tool calls while preserving provenance.

sections.title: Benchmark Comparison and Known vs Low-Confidence Gaps
sections.problem: Each benchmark measures one axis, so no single number tells you whether agents are deployable on real work.
sections.why: All three are proxies with known limitations, and confidence varies sharply by task type.
sections.how: Compare the three on scoring, multi-agent structure, resource constraints, and subjectivity, then list what is well established versus what remains low-confidence.
sections.detail:
The instructor compares the three benchmarks and separates confident from uncertain claims.

  • METR: automatically scored, no multi-agent interaction, no resource constraints, and not punishing of mistakes -- it targets single-agent, cleanly verifiable tasks.
  • GDPval: tasks are extremely well specified (the human's implicit context is written into the prompt) and one-shot, with no iterative correction; it requires tacit knowledge already in the model.
  • DeepScholarBench: fills the reference-data gap, exposing retrieval, foundational-paper, and verifiability failures.
  • Well established: models improve on isolated, well-specified tasks; SWE and ML research show the most progress; stronger models produce well-organized output even when parts are wrong.
  • Low confidence: context-heavy tasks, ambiguous prompts, adversarial environments, 95% reliability, generalization beyond software/knowledge work, and finding/verifying sources in a knowledge base.

sections.title: Final Synthesis: Forecasts, Reliability, Metrics
sections.problem: The exponential horizon story must be reconciled with the linear economic-value story, and it is unclear what to measure.
sections.why: Different metrics capture different progress; reliability and error recovery improve while performance stays task-dependent.
sections.how: Summarize METR's 7-month doubling and the 2028-2031 month-long-task forecast, contrast GDPval's linear 48% win rate, and prescribe duration-, economic-, and synthesis-quality metrics validated against humans.
sections.detail:
The closing synthesis ties the metrics together.

  • METR: a 7-month doubling of the horizon at 50% reliability, with a forecast that by 2028-2031 models will nearly complete one-month tasks.
  • GDPval: a much more linear improvement over two years, reaching about 48% win rate on some tasks while many categories remain low -- tempering the exponential story with real economic work.
  • Context/reference data is the recurring gap: many GDPval tasks require context or reference files, and DeepScholarBench shows quality and verifiability lagging humans.
  • Forecast: reliability and error recovery should keep improving, but performance will stay task-dependent; solving longer-horizon tasks does not guarantee reliable or high-quality outputs.
  • Metric prescription: we need duration-based, economic-value-based, and synthesis-quality-based metrics, each validated against humans who can actually solve the tasks.

sections.title: Open Q&A: Deployability, Long Tail, AI Co-Scientist
sections.problem: Practitioners ask whether current reliability makes agents deployable and what fundamentally blocks the long tail.
sections.why: The last 20% -- reliability and hard domains -- is far harder than the first 80%, and both data and model capability matter.
sections.how: Instructor answers on the long tail, clarifies that METR's 50% is an average of per-task success rates across attempts, and frames today's systems as AI co-scientists rather than autonomous AI scientists.
sections.detail:
The final Q&A ranges from deployability to career advice.

  • Long tail: the first 80% is easy and the last 20% takes a decade; hard domains such as distributed systems stay difficult. SWE and verified coding keep improving, but many non-PR tasks remain hard.
  • On the METR 50% number: it is the average of per-task success rates across attempts (e.g. across 97 tasks), so a 50% task means the answer is good about half the time.
  • Trajectory: timelines move fast and are hard to predict; today's systems are AI co-scientists -- strong brainstormers with broad knowledge -- not yet autonomous AI scientists that build the next generation of models.
  • What blocks the long tail: both data and fundamental model capability; robotics startups, for instance, bet on data collection to close the gap.
  • Closing advice: CS fundamentals remain valuable, and the durable skill is providing the model the context it needs.
